import { Meta } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'; import { ContrastStatus } from './_components/ContrastStatus'; # Marsh Design System Three things to know before you write any code here: 1. **Colors always go through a role, never a hex value.** `getRoleColor('interactive.primary')`, not `#000f47`. This is enforced by `npm run roles:check` in CI — see [Colors](?path=/docs/foundations-colors--docs). 2. **Layout is plain Tailwind grid utilities.** `grid grid-cols-12 gap-6`, not custom CSS. There's an older, unrelated grid system still used by a handful of legacy pages — if you're building something new, you don't need it. See [Grid](?path=/docs/foundations-grid--docs). 3. **Building UI? Check for an existing component first.** Every component in the current component library — buttons, forms, dialogs, tables, everything — is browsable with live examples and "use this / not that" guidance at `/design-system` (run the app, see below). Don't build something that already exists. ## Run it ```bash npm install npm run dev # the app, http://localhost:5173 npm run storybook # this documentation, http://localhost:6006 ``` ## Starting a new page 1. **Check `/design-system` first.** Does what you need already exist? Does an existing component's props already cover it (a new `variant`/`tone`/`size` beats a new component)? Can you compose two or three existing ones? Only build new as a last resort. 2. **Add a route.** `src/Router.tsx` is a flat list — lazy-import your page, add one ``. 3. **Build with what's in `src/components/ui/`**, laid out with Tailwind grid, colored with roles: ```tsx import { Card, CardHeader, CardTitle, CardContent } from '@/components/ui/card'; import { Button } from '@/components/ui/button'; import { getRoleColor } from '@/theme/roles'; export default function HelloPage() { return (
Hello
); } ``` That's the whole pattern: components from `@/components/ui/*`, `grid`/`gap-*` for layout, `getRoleColor()` for any color that isn't already baked into the component. No `sx` prop, no CSS Modules, no hex values. Full walkthrough, route to finish: **`docs/get-started/BUILD_YOUR_FIRST_PAGE.md`**. ## Beyond building pages The workflow above (`components/ui/*` + roles + Tailwind grid) covers most day-to-day work. This system also does several things that aren't visible from that workflow alone — easy to miss if you only ever look at the component docs: - **Testing** — every `.stories.tsx` file doubles as a real test, rendered in an actual Chromium browser via Playwright (`@storybook/addon-vitest`), not just a visual example — on top of the usual `jsdom` unit tests. No extra test files to write; `npm test` runs both. Full guide, including coverage and running it from Storybook's own UI: [Testing](?path=/docs/foundations-testing--docs). - **Figma Code Connect** — real component source shown directly in Figma Dev Mode, so a designer inspecting a component in Figma sees the actual React code, not a guess. Setup and mapping files: `docs/FIGMA_CODE_CONNECT_GUIDE.md`, `src/figma/*.figma.tsx`. - **MCP-driven Figma sync** — pulls live Figma Variables straight into an interactive session (via the Figma Desktop Bridge MCP server) and diffs them against the token values actually shipping in code — catches drift between what Figma says a color should be and what's real. Re-checkable anytime without a live Figma connection: `npm run tokens:check-figma` / `tokens:check-figma-semantic`, against the snapshots in `src/figma-variable-map.json` / `src/figma-variable-map-semantic.json`. `docs/FIGMA_PRIMITIVE_TOKEN_ASSESSMENT.md` and `docs/FIGMA_SEMANTIC_TOKEN_ASSESSMENT.md` are real worked examples of what this surfaces. - **`agents/design-system-agent`** — a separate, unattended pipeline: point it at one Figma component node, it builds an MDS-compliant, PR-ready component headlessly — for a webhook, CI job, or scheduled sweep, not interactive use. Enforces `CLAUDE.md`'s rules structurally (per-subagent filesystem permission allowlists), not just by convention. See its own `agents/design-system-agent/README.md`. ## Where things are - **[/design-system](http://localhost:5173/design-system)** (run `npm run dev` first) — every component in the current library, live, with guidance on which one to reach for and when. Start here for "how do I build X." - **`docs/get-started/DEVELOPERS.md`** — the fuller written guide: project structure, conventions, how to add a new page. - **This Storybook, `Foundations/*`** — the token, color, typography, spacing, elevation, and accessibility system in detail. - **Root `CLAUDE.md`** — the complete rules document (written for AI coding agents, but accurate and thorough for a human reading it too). ## Token contrast status Automated WCAG contrast check across the token set, regenerated on token changes: ```bash npm run tokens:contrast:badge # refresh after a token change ```

import { Meta } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks';

<Meta title="Foundations/Accessibility" />

# Accessibility

Accessibility is integral—not an afterthought. These guidelines summarize baseline expectations when building components.

## Color & Contrast
- Maintain WCAG AA contrast (4.5:1 for body, 3:1 for large text / UI affordances).
- Avoid using only color to convey meaning; pair with iconography or text.
- Validate themed variants in both light & dark backgrounds.

## Focus States
- All interactive elements must show a clearly visible focus ring (minimum 2px contrast outline or equivalent offset shadow).
- Don’t remove outlines without providing an accessible replacement.

## Keyboard Navigation
- Tab order follows DOM order; avoid tabindex greater than 0.
- Provide Escape to close modals, menus, popovers.
- Use Arrow key patterns for composite widgets (menus, listboxes, tablists).

## Roles & ARIA
- Prefer native elements first (`button`, `input`, `select`) before custom roles.
- When necessary, apply correct ARIA attributes (`aria-expanded`, `aria-selected`, `aria-live`) and keep them in sync with state.
- Avoid redundant roles on native elements (e.g. `role="button"` on a `button` element).

## Motion & Reduction
- Respect prefers-reduced-motion: offer non-animated or simplified transitions.
- Avoid large parallax / continuous motion in dashboards.

## Testing Checklist
- Can all primary flows be completed with keyboard only?
- Do interactive components announce purpose, state, and changes to assistive tech?
- Are error messages programmatically associated with inputs?
- Are focus traps correctly released when layers close?

Portfolio overview

{/* product */}

A new chapter

{/* marketing */} ``` These ship in the published package, so a consumer can write them in their own code — verified in `dist-pkg/styles.css` rather than assumed. ## `h1`–`h6`, level by level **The two scales do not align level-for-level, and they are not meant to.** | level | product — `text-h*` | marketing — `text-serif-h*` | |---|---|---| | `hero` | — | **40 → 72px**, Marsh Serif 400 | | `h1` | **30px**, Noto Sans **700** | **28 → 36px**, Marsh Serif **400** | | `h2` | **24px**, Noto Sans **700** | **24 → 28px**, Marsh Serif **400** | | `h3` | **20px**, Noto Sans **700** | **20 → 24px**, Marsh Serif **400** | | `h4` | **18px**, Noto Sans **600** | **18 → 20px**, Marsh Serif **400** | | `h5` | **16px**, Noto Sans **600** | **16 → 18px**, Marsh Serif **400** | | `h6` | **14px**, Noto Sans **600** | **14 → 16px**, Marsh Serif **400** | Three differences, each deliberate: **Weight.** Product headings are **700** at `h1`–`h3` and **600** at `h4`–`h6`; marketing is **400** throughout. A serif at a heavy weight is a combination nobody designed — `font-serif-expressive font-bold` is explicitly in the Don't list below. Product headings carry hierarchy by weight because they sit in dense, scannable UI; marketing carries it by size and whitespace. **Fluid vs fixed.** Marketing sizes are `clamp()` between a 360px and a 1536px viewport, so a hero headline scales with the page. Product sizes are **fixed** steps: a dashboard heading that reflows as you resize a window makes a data table feel unstable, and the viewport is usually a desktop anyway. Both are `rem`-based, so both respect the browser font-size setting (WCAG 1.4.4). At a 20px browser default every size above grows proportionally — that is the point, not a bug. **Where the product scale comes from.** `text-h1`…`text-h6` are the stock Tailwind steps — `text-3xl`, `text-2xl`, `text-xl`, `text-lg`, `text-base`, `text-sm` — with the face and weight attached. That is intentional: dashboard pages already wrote exactly those by hand (`text-2xl font-bold` in three places), so the classes change nothing visually and only stop the face and weight being re-chosen each time. `text-h1` at 30px is `text-3xl`, which is why it does not match the marketing `h1`'s 28–36px range. `text-serif-hero` has no product counterpart on purpose. A full-bleed 72px headline is a marketing device; a dashboard that needs one is probably a marketing page. **Pick by expression, not by element.** `PageHeading` renders an `

` at `text-2xl`, not `text-h1` — because that is what dashboard page titles already render at. The element is semantics; the class is appearance. ## Four dashboard roles, and only four A style earns a name **only when it bundles three or more decisions** you would otherwise re-derive every time. Below that bar Tailwind's own class is better: shorter, precise, and it tells you the size. `text-sm` beats a `text-data-cell` that resolves to `text-sm` and *removes* information. | class | resolves to | why it earns a name | |---|---|---| | `text-metric-value` | `text-3xl` + bold + tight tracking + tabular | nobody remembers tracking **and** tabular every time | | `text-data-header` | `text-xs` + semibold + wide tracking + uppercase | consolidates **five** independent takes that existed in `card`, `list`, `notifications-drawer`, `stepper` and `toast` | | `text-metric-delta` | `text-sm` + medium + tabular | | | `text-data-numeric` | `text-sm` + tabular | the deliberate two-decision exception: `tabular-nums` is the most-forgotten decision in a data product | Everything else uses the stock scale — `text-sm`, `font-medium`, `tracking-wide`. import { Meta } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'; import { listRoles, getRoleColor } from '../theme/roles'; # Roles Layer Roles are an intent-focused abstraction above semantic tokens. Components should prefer roles instead of referencing `semanticColors` or primitive tokens directly. This improves resilience when refactoring themes, adding new modes, or adjusting accessibility constraints. ## Why Roles? - Decouples component styling from raw semantic token names - Enables alternative mode mappings (e.g. high-contrast) without component churn - Provides a vocabulary aligning design + engineering (text.primary, surface.subtle, status.success) - Simplifies validation: we can test role → color resolution instead of every component path ## Role Directory Below is the current role map. Dark mode values are derived automatically via semantic dark overrides (if defined for the underlying semantic color). {listRoles().map(r => { const light = getRoleColor(r.role, { mode: 'light' }); const dark = getRoleColor(r.role, { mode: 'dark' }); // Translucent roles (border.subtle in dark) composite over their // backdrop by design — drawn on the white docs page they look like // nothing at all. Give those a split ground so the reader sees what the // value actually does in both modes. const isAlpha = (c) => /rgba|hsla/i.test(String(c)); const swatchStyle = (color) => ({ background: isAlpha(color) ? `linear-gradient(90deg, #ffffff 50%, #101010 50%)` : color, boxShadow: isAlpha(color) ? `inset 0 0 0 999px ${color}` : undefined, border: '1px solid #e2e2e4', borderRadius: 4, width: 52, height: 22, fontSize: 10, color: isAlpha(color) ? '#878787' : undefined, fontFamily: 'system-ui, sans-serif', display: 'flex', alignItems: 'center', justifyContent: 'center' }); return ( ); })}
Role Semantic Token Description Light Dark
{r.role} {r.semantic} {r.description}
{light}
{dark}
## Usage Example ```tsx import { getRoleColor } from 'src/theme/roles'; const Chip = ({ children }) => ( {children} ); ``` ## Choosing a border role Three border roles look interchangeable and are not: | Role | For | Contrast obligation | |------|-----|---------------------| | `border.default` | The edge of an interactive control — an input outline, a button border, anything a user acts on | **Gated at 3:1** (WCAG 1.4.11). Never swap it for a quieter token to soften a design. | | `border.subtle` | Hairline rules *inside* a surface the user is already in — table row separators, list dividers, the grid shell | None. It is decoration, not a boundary. Tracked informationally so it cannot drift so faint it stops separating anything. | | `border.strong` | Deliberate emphasis above the default weight | — | `border.subtle` is **translucent in dark mode** (`rgba(255,255,255,0.10)`), not a fixed grey. A hairline has to composite over whatever sits behind it — the page, a raised panel, a pinned cell — and one fixed value cannot be correct on all three. Drawing light mode's `#e3e3e3` on a near-black page produces the brightest line on the screen, which is the bug this replaced. ## Choosing a surface role `surface.raised` is a panel sitting *above* the page. In light it is the same white as `surface.default` — paper on paper needs no lift, the border does that work. In dark it is genuinely lighter (`#1a1a1a` against the `#101010` page), so a grid or card reads as a surface rather than a hole cut into the background. For a row's state, the roles are not interchangeable either: **selection** is `surface.selected` (a brand tint — a state the user caused), while **hover** and **striping** are `surface.subtle` (a neutral lift). Using `surface.accent` for selection is a mistake this codebase has already made: it is one unit away from `surface.subtle` in light, so selected and hovered rows rendered identically. ## Guidelines - Introduce a new role only when multiple components share the intent and a semantic token name would leak implementation. - Avoid duplicating semantic names as roles (e.g. no `textPrimary` role) — prefer `text.primary` pattern. - Mark deprecated roles in future via metadata and surface during validation. ## Next Steps Planned enhancements: 1. Snapshot test of role resolutions 2. Lint rule preventing direct primitive / semantic usage in components 3. High-contrast / alternative mode mapping demonstration ## Enforcement Ladder Governance phases and current status: | Phase | Mechanism | Status | |-------|-----------|--------| | 1 | Warn-only script (`npm run roles:check`) | Complete | | 2 | Strict mode opt-in (`npm run roles:check:strict`) | Complete | | 3 | Full CI gate (`governance:ci` in workflow) | Active | | 4 | ESLint rule (auto-fix suggestions) | Planned | All components now use roles (0 direct primitive/semantic references). CI fails on regressions via `governance:ci`. ## Contrast Governance All role foreground/background pairs are enforced in contrast tests. There is no monitored backlog. Introducing a new role pair should include an enforced contrast entry from day one unless there is a clearly documented incremental plan. _Last updated: full role contrast enforcement & CI gate active._

{/*
  This page documents BOTH spacing tracks on purpose.

  The previous version described only `theme.spacing(index)` — the MUI track —
  while all 73 components in src/components/ui use Tailwind utility classes.
  A developer reading it would not have found the API their component actually
  needs. The mapping table below is generated from `spacing.ts` so the two
  tracks cannot silently diverge in this document.
*/}

# Spacing

Everything in this system sits on a **4px grid**. There is one grid and two ways
to write it, because the component set spans two styling tracks.

The important thing to know up front: **Tailwind's default spacing scale is
already a 4px grid.** That is why `tailwind.config.js` does not extend
`spacing` — it does not need to. Every step in the MDS scale is reachable with
a stock Tailwind class, exactly.

Since the v4 upgrade the whole scale derives from one variable:

```css
--spacing: 0.25rem;                    /* 4px */
.p-4 { padding: calc(var(--spacing) * 4) }   /* 1rem */
```

Practically that means the entire grid can be retuned from a single value — a
denser build could set `--spacing: 0.1875rem` (3px) and every utility follows.
Nothing here does that today, and it should not be done casually, but it is
worth knowing the lever exists.

## Which API to use

| You are working on… | Use | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Laying out children** (the common case) | `Stack` / `Inline` | `<Stack gap={4}>` |
| A component in `src/components/ui/` (shadcn/Radix) | Tailwind utility classes | `className="p-4 gap-2"` |
| An MUI-based component or an `sx` prop | `theme.spacing(index)` | `sx={{ p: 3, gap: 2 }}` |

All three land on the same pixel values. Do not convert between them by hand —
use the table below.

**Prefer `Stack`/`Inline` when you are spacing siblings.** They take the same
scale, but as a *type*: `gap={7}` (28px — not a step) is a compile error,
whereas `className="gap-7"` compiles happily and is quietly 4px off. See
**Components → Stack**.

## The scale

`spacing[i]` is **index-based**; the Tailwind class is **named for the pixel
value ÷ 4**. This is the single most common source of confusion: `spacing[3]`
is 16px, and 16px is `p-4`, not `p-3`.

<TokenTable
  columns={[
    { key: 'index', label: 'spacing[i]', width: 90 },
    { key: 'value', label: 'px', width: 55 },
    { key: 'rem', label: 'rem', width: 70 },
    { key: 'tw', label: 'Tailwind', width: 85 },
    { key: 'mui', label: 'MUI sx', width: 80 },
    { key: 'visual', label: 'Visual' }
  ]}
  rows={spacing.map((v, i) => ({
    index: i,
    value: v,
    rem: `${v / 16}rem`,
    tw: `p-${v / 4}`,
    mui: `p: ${i}`,
    visual: <div style={{ width: v, height: 12, background: '#002c77', borderRadius: 2 }} />
  }))}
  caption="All 15 MDS steps map exactly onto stock Tailwind classes — no config extension required. rem values assume the browser default 16px root, which this app does not override."
/>

### px or rem — they are not interchangeable here

The two tracks emit **different units**, and that has a real consequence:

| Track | What it emits | Under a user font-size change |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tailwind (`p-4`) | `padding: 1rem` | **Scales** with the user's setting |
| MUI (`sx={{ p: 3 }}`) | `padding: 16px` | **Fixed** |

`spacing.ts` stores plain numbers and `src/theme.ts`'s `spacingFn` appends
`px`, so every MUI-spaced component is pinned to absolute pixels while every
shadcn component reflows. A user who raises their browser font size gets a
layout where half the components grow and half do not.

That matters for **WCAG 1.4.4 (Resize Text)**. It is not a defect in either
track on its own — it is a consequence of the two coexisting, and it is worth
knowing before choosing which to build a new dense layout in. Prefer the
Tailwind track for anything text-adjacent.

The `rem` column above is the conversion: divide px by 16.

## One scale, many utilities

The same 15 steps drive every spacing utility — padding, margin, gap, and the
sizing/inset families. Picking a step is one decision; which property you apply
it to is another.

| Family | Tailwind | MUI `sx` | Used here |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Gap (flex/grid) | `gap-4` `gap-x-2` `gap-y-6` | `gap: 3` | **231** |
| Padding, all sides | `p-4` | `p: 3` | 90 |
| Padding, axis | `px-4` `py-2` | `px: 3` `py: 1` | 177 |
| Padding, one side | `pt-2` `pr-3` `pb-2` `pl-3` | `pt: 1` … | 42 |
| Margin, all sides | `m-4` | `m: 3` | — |
| Margin, axis | `mx-auto` `my-4` | `mx: 'auto'` `my: 3` | 7 |
| Margin, one side | `mt-4` `mb-2` | `mt: 3` `mb: 1` | 65 |
| Space between children | `space-y-2` `space-x-4` | — | 8 |

Counts are live usage in `src/components/ui/`.

### Prefer `gap` over margins

`gap-*` outnumbers every margin utility here roughly three to one, and that is
the house style rather than an accident. Gap spaces children from the parent, so
it cannot collapse, cannot double up against a sibling's margin, and leaves no
stray trailing space on the last child. Reach for a flex or grid container with
`gap-*` before adding `mb-*` to a list of items.

Margins are still right for pushing a single element away from its neighbours —
`mt-*` on a section heading, `mb-*` on a standalone block. Both are in the
system; the ordering is a default, not a prohibition.

Negative margins (`-mt-2`, `-mx-4`) exist and are used sparingly — 5 occurrences,
all for deliberate overlap such as pulling a border flush. They are legitimate
but should be commented where they appear.

### Physical vs logical properties

Tailwind offers both physical (`ml-` `mr-` `pl-` `pr-`) and logical
(`ms-` `me-` `ps-` `pe-`) directions. Logical properties flip automatically in
right-to-left locales; physical ones do not.

**Today this system uses 64 physical and 0 logical.** That is fine while every
consumer is left-to-right, and it is the single thing that would need changing
first if a right-to-left market is ever in scope. New components should prefer
`ms-`/`me-`/`ps-`/`pe-` where the choice is arbitrary, so the retrofit shrinks
rather than grows.

## Dense half-steps

Tailwind's default scale also offers **2px half-steps** (`1.5`, `2.5`, `3.5`)
that the MDS index scale does not contain. These are **permitted in dense,
list-like UI** — menu items, table rows, drawer rows, chips — where 4px is too
tight and 8px too loose.

| Class | px | rem | Where it is appropriate |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `p-1.5` | 6px | `0.375rem` | Menu and dropdown items, compact chips |
| `p-2.5` | 10px | `0.625rem` | Table cells at compact density, drawer rows |
| `p-3.5` | 14px | `0.875rem` | Rare — prefer `p-3` (12px) or `p-4` (16px) first |

They are a deliberate sub-scale, not an escape hatch. Reach for a full step
first; use a half-step only when the full step is visibly wrong.

## What not to do

- **No arbitrary values.** `p-[13px]`, `gap-[7px]` and similar bypass the grid
  entirely. This is now **enforced** — see below.
- **Do not hand-convert between the tracks.** `spacing[6]` is 32px is `p-8`.
  Guessing produces `p-6` (24px) and a layout that is one step out.
- **Do not add a step to `spacing.ts` casually.** The scale is deliberately
  curated — 4px micro-steps at the small end, widening to 16px intervals at the
  large end. See the token request process before extending it.

## Enforcement

`npm run composition:check` reports, and `composition:check:strict` **fails**
CI (via `governance:ci`) on two things:

| Rejected | Why | Instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `p-[16px]`, `gap-[8px]` | An arbitrary value is a scale step spelled so it bypasses the scale | `p-4`, `gap-2` |
| `gap-7` (28px), `pr-9` (36px) | Compiles fine; not a value in `spacing.ts` | `gap-6`/`gap-8`, `pr-8`/`pr-10` |

`p-[var(--x)]` is allowed — reading a token is the sanctioned use of an
arbitrary value.

When the check was first run it found 20 arbitrary values and 5 off-scale
steps, including `gap-[8px]` five times. Those are fixed; the gate keeps them
fixed.

**Escape hatches:** `spacing-allow` on the line, `spacing-allow-file` in the
file. Legitimate for values derived from a control's **geometry** — the 28px
indent aligning checkbox helper text under its label, the 36px padding
clearing a calendar icon button — but not for dodging a spacing decision.
Say which in the comment.

A third check is **advisory and never fails**: physical properties
(`ml-`/`mr-`/`pl-`/`pr-`) over logical ones (`ms-`/`me-`/`ps-`/`pe-`).
Currently 61 physical, 0 logical. That number should shrink, not grow.

## Layout guidance

- Container padding: **16 / 24 / 32** (`p-4` / `p-6` / `p-8`) by breakpoint.
- Vertical rhythm in dense panels: multiples of **8** (`gap-2`, `gap-4`).
- Dashboard section gutters: **32–48** (`gap-8` … `gap-12`).
- Compact table rows: **6–10** via the half-steps above.
- Stacks and lists: a flex/grid parent with `gap-*`, not `mb-*` on each child —
  or better, `<Stack gap={n}>`, which cannot drift off-scale.
- Starting a whole page? Use the `PageShell` template rather than rebuilding
  the frame. See **Components → PageShell**.

### Control heights

Every interactive control — buttons *and* fields — shares one height scale,
defined in `src/components/ui/control-size.ts`:

| `size` | Height | Padding | Type | Icon |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `sm` | 32px (`h-8`) | `px-2.5` | `text-sm` | 14px |
| `md` | 40px (`h-10`) | `px-3` | `text-sm` | 16px |
| `lg` | 48px (`h-12`) | `px-4` | `text-base` | 20px |

The rule this enforces: **a control and a button declaring the same size are
the same height.** They constantly sit side by side — filter bars, search
rows, button groups — and nothing else checks it.

It did not hold before. `size="md"` meant 48px on a Button and 40px on an
Input and Select, so the button towered over the fields in every such row.
Four more controls (Textarea, Combobox, DatePicker, InputOTP) had no size
prop at all and had drifted to 40px, 32px and 40px respectively. The scale
now lives in one file and every control reads from it; a height defined
privately inside one component's cva block is how that drift started.

Two deliberate exclusions:

- **Textarea** takes the padding and type but no fixed height — its height
  comes from content and `rows`.
- **Checkbox, Radio, Switch** sit on their own scale. They are glyphs, not
  text boxes, and stretching them to 40px would look broken.

Grouped controls cascade: `<ButtonGroup size="sm">` and `<InputGroup size="sm">`
publish the size through context, so children inherit it and a group with a
mismatched child is not expressible by accident. A child's own `size` still
wins for the deliberate exception.

### Form rhythm

Forms are the densest nesting in the system, so the steps are fixed and
deliberately **tighten inward**:

| Level | Component | Class | px |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Section — legend ↔ groups | `FieldSet` | `gap-6` | 24 |
| Between fields | `FieldGroup` | `gap-5` | 20 |
| Label ↔ control | `Field` | `gap-3` | 12 |
| Label ↔ description | `FieldContent` | `gap-1.5` | 6 |

Two constraints produced these, and both matter if you ever revisit them:

1. **Outer must be ≥ inner.** `FieldGroup` previously used `gap-7` (28px),
   which was *looser* than the `FieldSet` (24px) containing it — so fields
   read as less related to each other than to the heading above them.
2. **Inter-field spacing must stay clear of the field's own 12px internal
   gap.** At 20px the ratio is ~1.7×, enough to keep field boundaries
   legible. 16px (1.3×) was tested and rejected: it starts to blur which
   label belongs to which input.

Checkbox and radio groups collapse to `gap-3` (12px) at both levels, because
their rows are single-line and do not need field-sized separation.
- Genuinely two-dimensional layout belongs in grid utilities, not nested
  stacks — see **Foundations → Grid**.

## Corner radius

Radius uses **Tailwind's stock scale, unmodified**. Nothing is overridden; what
this system adds is *intent* — which step means what — enforced in CI.

| Class | px | Use |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `rounded-none` | 0 | Flush edges, table cells |
| **`rounded-sm`** | **4** | **The control default.** Buttons, inputs, selects, comboboxes, date fields |
| `rounded-md` | 6 | Chips, cells, menu items and other small surfaces |
| `rounded-lg` | 8 | Badges, menu items, small surfaces |
| `rounded-xl` | 12 | Cards, the data-grid shell, dialogs |
| `rounded-2xl` | 16 | Large feature surfaces |
| `rounded-full` | — | Pills, avatars |

`rounded-full` and `rounded-none` are keywords, not steps. `rounded-xs`,
`rounded-sm`, `rounded-3xl` and `rounded-4xl` are valid Tailwind but **rejected
here** — a fifth and sixth corner size is how a scale stops being a scale.

### The 2px era, and why it ended

The system ran on a **2px** radius for its first year: small, squared-off, and
a deliberate part of an institutional, precise feel. It was raised in
**September 2026** — softer surfaces, crisper contents — after a visual review
against contemporary data-grid references found the old value was the single
largest contributor to the system reading as dated.

This was a brand decision, not a tidy-up. If it is ever revisited, revisit it
as one.

### Why nothing is overridden — two failures, not one

**First failure.** `tailwind.config.js` used to rescale `borderRadius` around a
`--radius` variable, because shadcn's defaults assume `0.5rem`. It computed
`rounded-md` as `calc(2px - 2px)` = **0** and drove `rounded-sm` negative, so
roughly **110 components silently rendered square** while their class names
said otherwise.

**Second failure.** The fix for that was an `@theme` block redefining
`--radius-xs` … `--radius-xl` with this system's own values. It held the ladder
monotonic, but it made our class names disagree with the entire ecosystem:
`rounded-lg` meant 12px here and 8px everywhere else, so any snippet copied
from shadcn or the Tailwind docs rendered at the wrong size with no error. And
because `src/styles.package.css` shipped that block, it **redefined `rounded-*`
inside every consuming application** — the same category of mistake as a
library imposing its own CSS reset.

The stock scale already contains four of the five values this system needs, so
neither workaround is necessary. The fifth (10px, for popovers) had exactly two
call sites and was dropped to 8px.

**Do not reintroduce a `borderRadius` override, and do not redeclare
`--radius-*` in `@theme`.** Both are gated.

### The trade-off, stated plainly

There is no single lever any more. Moving the brand radius means a scripted
rename across ~190 call sites rather than editing one variable. That is a real
cost, accepted deliberately: a design system's radius changes rarely, the
rename is mechanical and gate-verified, and the alternative was redefining
words that belong to Tailwind.

### What is gated

`npm run radius:check` (in `governance:ci`) fails on:

- an **arbitrary** radius (`rounded-[7px]`) or the **bare `rounded`** utility —
  Tailwind inlines both, so they answer to nothing;
- a step **outside the four sanctioned ones**, inside `src/components/ui`;
- `src/index.css` or `src/styles.package.css` **reintroducing a `--radius-*`
  override**;
- **this table** disagreeing with those values.

Before this gate existed, nothing in the repo inspected radius at all — not a
script, not a test — so the 2px→6px change would have been invisible to CI.

## Where the values live

- `src/spacing.ts` — the canonical array, exported as `spacing` and consumed by
  the MUI theme's `spacing` function (`src/theme.ts`).
- `dist/tokens.json` — the same 15 steps, exported under `spacing` for Figma and
  non-React consumers.
- Tailwind — **not configured**, because its default scale already matches. If
  the MDS scale ever gains a step that is not a multiple of 4px, Tailwind will
  need an explicit `extend.spacing` entry at that point.

import { Meta } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'; # Grid System The standard grid for all new work: plain [Tailwind CSS](https://tailwindcss.com/docs/grid-template-columns) grid utilities. No custom classes, no separate import — `grid`, `grid-cols-*`, `gap-*`, and `col-span-*` are built into Tailwind itself and already available everywhere in this app.

Which grid do I use?

Building anything new, including any src/components/ui (shadcn) component? Use this page. Editing one of the existing legacy MUI marketing pages/sections (HeroBanner, MarshCorporate, the marsh-new-charpter-begins and CorporateLandingPage sections)? Those already use a different, older grid system — see Foundations/Grid Legacy instead, and don't mix the two on the same element.

import { GridHealth } from './_components/GridHealth'; --- ## For Designers ### What this gives you - A 12-column grid at any breakpoint, with `col-span-*` to size an element across N columns - A spacing scale from 0 to 24rem (`gap-0` through `gap-96`, on the same 4px base as the rest of the design system) - Five responsive breakpoints, applied with a prefix (`md:grid-cols-4`), not a suffix - Auto-fit/auto-fill columns for card grids where you don't know the count in advance - A centered `container` utility, customized for this brand to cap at 1540px (matching the legacy system's own max width, so pages don't visually jump if they mix eras) ### Design tokens ``` Breakpoints (real Tailwind defaults — unmodified in this project): sm: 640px md: 768px lg: 1024px xl: 1280px 2xl: 1536px Container (tailwind.config.js — the one customization in this system): centered: yes padding: 16px (default) → 24px (md) → 32px (lg) 2xl cap: 1540px ← note: not 1536px. The container's own max-width is set slightly wider than the bare 2xl breakpoint, to match the legacy grid's 1540px container exactly. Spacing scale (gap-N — 0.25rem/4px base, same grid as everywhere else in MDS): gap-0: 0px gap-4: 16px gap-12: 48px gap-24: 96px gap-1: 4px gap-5: 20px gap-14: 56px gap-32: 128px gap-2: 8px gap-6: 24px gap-16: 64px gap-40: 160px gap-3: 12px gap-8: 32px gap-20: 80px gap-48: 192px ``` --- ## For Developers ### Nothing to install Tailwind's grid utilities are generated on demand from whatever classes appear in your JSX — there's no import, no SCSS `@use`, no separate build step. Just write the class names. ```tsx // No import needed — Tailwind scans src/**/*.{ts,tsx} automatically
...
``` ### The one real customization `tailwind.config.js`'s `theme.container` is customized so the `container` utility centers, applies the same 16/24/32px padding steps the rest of this app uses, and caps at exactly **1540px** at the `2xl` tier — everything else (`grid-cols-*`, `gap-*`, the `sm/md/lg/xl/2xl` breakpoints themselves) is stock Tailwind, unmodified. --- ## Grid, Stack, or PageShell? Three tools, and picking the wrong one is the usual cause of layout that fights back: | Situation | Use | Why | | --- | --- | --- | | Children in **one direction** with even spacing | `` / `` | The gap is type-checked against the DS scale; `gap={7}` will not compile | | **Two-dimensional** layout — columns that reflow, spans, ordering | Grid utilities on this page | A grid is what this is. Three nested stacks faking one is harder to read and to change | | The **page frame** — header, sidebar, main | `` | It already handles the responsive sidebar, the mobile scrim, and the `min-w-0` chain that stops wide tables scrolling the page sideways | `Stack` and grid compose freely: a `Stack` of sections where one section is a `grid grid-cols-3` is the normal shape of a dashboard page. --- ## Common Patterns ### Pattern 1 — Two-column layout (main + sidebar) **When to use**: main content + sidebar layouts, the most common page shape. ```tsx
Main content
Sidebar
```
Main Content

66% width from md up, 100% below

Sidebar

33% width from md up, 100% below

--- ### Pattern 2 — Responsive card grid, auto-fit **When to use**: product cards, blog posts, image galleries — any count of cards, unknown in advance. ```tsx
{products.map((product) => )}
```
{Array.from({ length: 6 }).map((_, i) => (
Card {i + 1}

Auto-fits at 220px min

))}
Tailwind doesn't ship a bare `auto-fit` utility (the column-min-width is arbitrary per layout), so this is the one pattern that reaches for an inline `gridTemplateColumns` — everything else on this page is plain classes. --- ### Pattern 3 — Dashboard with variable-height widgets **When to use**: analytics dashboards, admin panels with widgets of different heights. ```tsx
```
Tall Widget (2 rows)
Metric A
Full Height (3 rows)
Metric B
Wide Widget (2 columns)
--- ### Pattern 4 — Sidebar layout (fixed + flexible) **When to use**: app shells, documentation sites, admin panels. ```tsx
```
Sidebar

Fixed 250px from md up

Main Content

Flexible width

Tailwind's arbitrary-value syntax (`grid-cols-[250px_1fr]`) covers the legacy system's `.grid-cols-sidebar` preset — there's no need for a named utility for a one-off column template. --- ### Pattern 5 — Column ordering (responsive reorder) **When to use**: show content first on mobile, sidebar first on desktop, without changing DOM order. ```tsx
```

Second on mobile, first from md up

Sidebar

First on mobile, second from md up

Note the direction — this example deliberately shows main content ordered *after* sidebar in source but *first* visually below `md`, the opposite of Pattern 1. Reorder visually only; keep source order logical for screen readers. --- ## Complete Utility Reference | Category | Classes | |---|---| | Container | `grid` | | Columns | `grid-cols-{1-12}`, `col-span-{1-12}`, `col-span-full`, `col-start-{1-13}`, `col-end-{1-13}` | | Rows | `grid-rows-{1-6}`, `row-span-{1-6}`, `row-span-full`, `row-start-{1-7}`, `row-end-{1-7}` | | Gap | `gap-{N}`, `gap-x-{N}`, `gap-y-{N}` (full spacing scale, 0–96) | | Flow | `grid-flow-row`, `grid-flow-col`, `grid-flow-dense`, `grid-flow-row-dense`, `grid-flow-col-dense` | | Alignment (items) | `items-start`, `items-center`, `items-end`, `items-baseline`, `items-stretch` | | Alignment (content) | `justify-start`, `justify-center`, `justify-end`, `justify-between`, `justify-around`, `justify-evenly` | | Combined placement | `place-items-{start\|center\|end\|stretch\|baseline}`, `place-content-{start\|center\|end\|between\|around\|evenly\|stretch}` | | Ordering | `order-{1-12}`, `order-first`, `order-last`, `order-none` | | Aspect ratio | `aspect-square`, `aspect-video`, `aspect-[N/M]` (arbitrary ratios) | | Container | `container` (customized max-width, see above) | | Responsive prefix | `sm:`, `md:`, `lg:`, `xl:`, `2xl:` — prepend to any class above | Any class not covered by a named utility (an unusual column template, a one-off ratio) is available via Tailwind's arbitrary-value syntax: `grid-cols-[200px_1fr_200px]`, `aspect-[21/9]`. --- ## import { Meta } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'; # Grid System — Legacy A Bootstrap-inspired 12-column grid system built with CSS Grid. This is the **older** of the two grid systems in this codebase, kept for the existing pages/sections that already depend on it.

⚠️ Not for new work

All new components (including everything in src/components/ui) use plain Tailwind grid utilities instead — see Foundations/Grid. This page documents the older, Bootstrap-style system still used by ~26 existing legacy MUI marketing pages/sections (HeroBanner, MarshCorporate, the marsh-new-charpter-begins and CorporateLandingPage sections, and a few others). Every class below carries an mds-legacy- prefix — added when these names were found to collide with identically-named Tailwind utilities, since both systems load globally in the same app. Never mix the two systems' classes on the same element.

Columns: 12 (+ custom 1-12)
Base Unit: 4px
Gutters: 8px-128px
Breakpoints: xs→xxl (1540px)
Aspect Ratios: 6 utilities

import { Meta } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks'; # Choosing a table Three components render tabular data, and the difference between two of them is **not** what they can do. Reading their story lists side by side will not tell you which to reach for, so this page does.

Table

A simple, read-oriented table. Its own implementation — no TanStack, no shared engine.

Prefer DataTable for new work. See “Table’s future” below.

DataTable

The default choice. Pass props, get a table. Every capability the grid has is reachable through an enable* prop.

DataGrid

The same engine, composed. Reach for it when you need the table instance — not when you need more features.

## The thing that confuses everyone **`DataTable` and `DataGrid` are the same component with two API shapes.** `DataTable` imports `DataGrid` and renders it. It is a preset, not a lesser tier. There is no capability in one that is missing from the other — sorting, filtering, selection, pinning, reordering, resizing, virtualization, inline editing, cell ranges and clipboard are all available either way. So the question is never *“do I need more power?”*. It is: > **Does anything outside the table need to read or drive its state?** | | `DataTable` | `DataGrid` | | --- | --- | --- | | API | ~28 props | composed children | | Who owns the table instance | the component | **you** | | Read selection / filters / sorting directly | no — only via callbacks | yes | | Reorder, replace or omit parts | no | yes | | Capabilities | identical | identical | **Use `DataTable`** unless one of these is true: - a toolbar, header or side panel outside the table needs to read its state; - you need to drive the table from elsewhere (a saved view, a URL, another control); - you need to replace a part, or leave one out; - you want the toolbar somewhere other than above the table. **Then use `DataGrid`**, and see its `ConsumerOwnedState` story — that one story is the entire reason this API exists. ## Reading the stories Because the two share an engine, several stories necessarily look alike. What each set is *for*: - **`Components/DataTable`** — the preset. Props in, table out. This is where capabilities are demonstrated: selection, column visibility, server pagination, inline editing, the state variants. - **`Components/DataGrid`** — composition. How the parts assemble, and what becomes possible once you hold the instance. - **`Components/Table`** — the simple table. Nothing here is unique to it. A story appearing in both places is showing the same behaviour through two APIs, not two behaviours. ## Table’s future `Table` shares no code with the other two. Every fix has to be made twice, and its capabilities were deliberately ported to the grid so it could be retired — see the `capabilities ported from table.tsx` suite in `data-grid-edges.test.tsx`. **It is now deprecated** — since 0.7.0, removed after 0.8.0 (2026-12-23). The last capability it had that the grid lacked was an opening sort, now `initialSorting`, and as of 2026-09-26 it has **zero consumers**: the four app surfaces and the Figma Code Connect mapping all point at `DataTable`. It is not deleted yet, deliberately. `Table` has been a published export since 0.6.0 while its deprecation reads *"since 0.7.0"* — a version that has never shipped — so no consumer has actually been warned. Removing it now would break an API nobody was told about. It goes when 0.7.0 has carried the warning and 0.8.0 arrives. ### The markup primitives The tier `Table` was pretending to be. `TableHeader`, `TableBody`, `TableFooter`, `TableRow`, `TableHead`, `TableCell` and `TableCaption` are exported now; the `Table` root itself joins them when the legacy engine is removed, because it currently owns that name. ```tsx PolicyPremium Commercial Auto$12,400
``` They carry this system's styling and nothing else — no state, no sorting, no pagination. `DataGrid` is their first consumer, which is what keeps them honest: header height, cell padding and the type scale are defined there once rather than restated in the grid. The evidence that this was overdue: the ambiguous `aria-label="Select all rows"` and the positional `Select row N` were both fixed on the grid, and both still sit in `table.tsx`, because nothing connects the two implementations. It also has zero tests, against roughly ninety on the grid. Migrating: | `Table` | `DataTable` | | --- | --- | | `variant="bordered"` | the default — `DataGridContainer` draws it | | `variant="borderless"` | `` | | `variant="striped"` | `striped` | | `variant="compact"` / `size` | `defaultDensity="compact"` | | `defaultSortColumn` + `defaultSortDirection` | `initialSorting={[{ id, desc }]}` | | `emptyMessage` | `emptyState` | | `onRowSelect` | `enableRowSelection` + `onSelectionChange` | Two props do **not** carry over, deliberately: `hoverable={false}` (a row you can interact with should say so) and `onSort` (with `DataGrid` you hold the instance and can read sorting directly, which is strictly more capable than a callback). ## When not to use a table at all Tables exist so people can compare the same attributes across many records. If that is not the task, something else is usually better: - one record at a time → a detail view; - few comparable attributes → a list or cards; - hierarchy matters more than comparison → a tree; - trend matters more than values → a chart.

<Meta title="Foundations/Contrast" />

# Contrast Quality

<ContrastStatus />

This page centralizes the automated contrast governance for the design system.

## What The Badge Means
The badge reflects the current result of the local WCAG contrast audit across both light and dark modes:
- PASS: All required (non-informational) token pairs meet or exceed their ratio thresholds.
- FAIL: One or more required pairs fall below threshold (investigate before merging).
- INFO: One or more informational pairs were included (optional) and may not meet ratios; these do not fail CI unless explicitly enforced.

Informational pairs are intentionally unrealistic or context-dependent (e.g., accent-on-surface where that combination is never directly rendered as text/background in a real component) but tracked for visibility.

## Regenerating The Badge
```bash
npm run tokens:contrast:badge
```
Generates / updates two artifacts at repo root:
- `contrast-badge.svg` (display asset)
- `contrast-badge.json` (structured badge payload)

## Full Contrast Report
Produce a structured JSON report of every pair in all modes:
```bash
npm run tokens:contrast:json > contrast-report.json
```
Or with informational pairs expanded in terminal output:
```bash
npm run tokens:contrast:info
```

## Typical Workflow
1. Adjust primitive or semantic tokens.
2. Run `npm run tokens:check` (builds, validates, contrast checks).
3. If a contrast failure appears, tweak semantic dark overrides (preferred) or primitives (only if widely beneficial).
4. Regenerate badge if merging a meaningful change.

## CI Behavior
The GitHub Action consumes the JSON report and annotates failures. Informational pairs are excluded unless the flag `--include-informational` is added. The workflow can be extended later to comment on PRs with a diff summary.

## Future Enhancements (Planned)
- Per-token historical trend (sparkline) by persisting past reports.
- PR comment summarizing changed contrast statuses.
- Live interactive contrast playground (token picker + backgrounds).

## Role-Level Contrast (Full Enforcement)
Role contrast is validated in `roles.contrast.test.ts`. All tracked role foreground/background pairs now meet or exceed required ratios in both light and dark modes.

Current status:
- 100% of role pairs enforced (0 monitored)
- Interactive primary (onAccent text) and all status pairs were the final items promoted after dark mode adjustments

Governance implications:
- Any regression in required contrast now fails tests, the governance script (`npm run governance:ci`), and CI.
- To introduce a new pair iteratively, you can temporarily reintroduce a monitored section in the test and governance script—but the default expectation is full enforcement.

If future visual refinements create temporary contrast dips, prefer adjusting dark overrides rapidly rather than reclassifying pairs as monitored.

---

import { Meta } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks';

<Meta title="Foundations/Documentation-Guidelines" />

# Documentation Guidelines

This page defines how we write and structure design system documentation (MDX + Autodocs).

## Core Principles
1. Single source of truth: component APIs live in CSF stories (Autodocs); conceptual & foundational narratives live in MDX.
2. Keep MDX mostly narrative; move logic & rendering complexity into imported React helper components.
3. Prefer semantic clarity over visual cleverness—docs should be skimmable and linkable.

## Markdown / MDX Standard
We follow **GitHub Flavored Markdown (GFM)** where compatible with MDX.

Reference spec: https://github.github.com/gfm/

### Supported GFM Features We Use
- Tables (for tokens, comparison, matrices).
- Fenced code blocks with language hints (` ```tsx ` etc.).
- Autolinks & inline code spans.
- Task lists (only in contributor docs / not rendered inside Storybook nav yet) for internal checklists.

### Features to Avoid or Use Sparingly
- Raw HTML tags (e.g. `<button>`) inside prose—prefer backticks (`button`) to avoid parse edge cases.
- Deep nested lists (harder to scan). Flatten content or break into new sections.
- Excessive inline styling; use components or theme tokens.

## MDX Structure Rules
- Each MDX page must export a single `meta` object at the top with a `title`.
- Heading order: one `#` (title) then `##` level sections. Do not skip levels.
- Place future work / TODO notes in an italic block at bottom (`_Future: ..._`).
- Import helper components from `./_components/*` or root tokens (e.g. `../spacing`).
- Keep frontmatter out (not needed with Storybook’s indexer).

## Autodocs Integration
For components:
1. Add `tags: ['autodocs']` in the CSF default export (if you want the autogenerated docs tab).
2. Our authored MDX pages use a Controls‑only approach (no separate `ArgsTable` / `ArgTypes` blocks) because Controls already surfaces prop name, description, default & live editing.
3. Use the shared `<ApiSection />` component instead of manually placing `<Controls />` and variant `<Story />` blocks.
4. Only create a bespoke MDX page if narrative complexity (patterns, anti‑patterns, accessibility guidance) justifies it.

### ApiSection Usage Pattern
```mdx
// import { Story } from '@storybook/blocks';
// import * as ButtonStories from '../../components/Button/Button.stories';
// import { ApiSection } from '../Components/ApiSection';

// export const meta = { title: 'Components/Button' };

## Examples
<Story of={ButtonStories.Primary} />
<Story of={ButtonStories.Secondary} />

## Playground
<ApiSection primary={ButtonStories.Primary} variants={[ButtonStories.Secondary, ButtonStories.Danger]} />
```
Guidelines:
- Pass the primary (most representative) story to `primary`.
- List only meaningful variant stories in `variants` (avoid noise like trivial arg permutations).
- Omit `variants` if the component has a single canonical presentation.

## Referencing Stories in MDX
Prefer module/story references over string IDs:
`<Story of={ButtonStories.Primary} />` instead of `<Story id="components-button--primary" />`.
IDs are brittle during renames; story exports are refactor‑safe.

## Design Tokens
Tokens are code-first. MDX should render them dynamically so docs always match code (`ColorSwatches`, `TypographyTable`, `ElevationGrid`). Avoid copying values manually into tables.

## Accessibility Content
When documenting patterns, prefer: guidance list → example → counter-example (DO / DON’T) — plan a small `<DoDont />` block component for future expansion.

## Linting & Quality (Planned)
- Add a docs lint script to enforce: single `<Meta>`, no `<Story id=...>`, no deprecated `ArgsTable` / `ArgTypes` usage, heading depth.
- Visual regression (Chromatic) will track design token component diffs.

## Changelog Discipline
Any breaking token rename or removal must: (1) update token source file, (2) update affected MDX narrative, (3) annotate change in `CHANGELOG.md` under a Docs section.

## Quick Author Checklist
- [ ] File name ordered (e.g. `70-NewTopic.mdx`).
- [ ] Single `<Meta>`.
- [ ] Uses `<ApiSection>` (no manual `<Controls>` unless a special case).
- [ ] No raw HTML tags in prose.
- [ ] Logic refactored to helper component if > ~10 lines.
- [ ] Uses story `of={...}` references, not `id=`.
- [ ] Tokens pulled from source, not hard-coded.
- [ ] Future TODO (if applicable) placed at bottom.

---

import { Meta } from '@storybook/addon-docs/blocks';

<Meta title="Foundations/Testing" />

# Testing

Everything a developer needs to run this repo's tests — locally, from inside Storybook itself, and in CI — in one place. The full command reference also lives in the README's Testing section; this page is the fuller walkthrough, including the Storybook-UI paths that don't have a CLI equivalent.

## The two test suites

`vitest.config.ts` defines two Vitest **projects** — both run whenever you run "the tests," but they test different things in different environments:

| Project | Environment | What it covers |
|---|---|---|
| `unit` | jsdom | Component behavior, hooks, utilities — anything under `src/__tests__/`, `*.unit.test.ts(x)`, `src/components/**/*.test.tsx`, `src/utils/**/*.test.tsx` |
| `storybook` | Real Chromium, via Playwright (`@storybook/addon-vitest`) | Every `.stories.tsx` file in the repo, rendered for real — not jsdom, not a mock DOM |

The `storybook` project is the important one to understand if you're used to writing separate test files: **you don't write a test for a story — the story *is* the test.** Any `.stories.tsx` you add is automatically picked up and rendered as a real browser test with zero extra setup. Interaction tests (`play` functions) run as part of the same pass.

## Running tests

```bash
npm test                              # both projects
npm run test:watch                    # both projects, watch mode
npx vitest run --project unit         # just the unit suite
npx vitest run --project storybook    # just the stories, as real browser tests
```

**Cold-cache note:** the first `storybook`-project run after clearing `node_modules/.cache/storybook` can show transient "Failed to fetch dynamically imported module" failures — Vite's dependency pre-bundling racing under load, not a real failure. A second run passes cleanly. If you hit this in CI, retry once or add a cache-warming step first.

## Coverage

Coverage tells you which lines of your actual source code your tests exercised — and, more usefully, which they *didn't*.

```bash
npm run test:coverage              # both projects combined — one number per file
npm run test:coverage:storybook    # storybook project only — coverage from stories alone
```

The distinction matters: `test:coverage` mixes together whatever a story touched *and* whatever a plain unit test touched into a single per-file percentage. If you specifically want to know "how much of this component's code do its stories alone exercise" — useful for a policy like "every component needs a story that covers most of it" — use the `:storybook` variant instead; the combined number can't isolate that.

### From inside Storybook itself

You don't need the CLI for this. In Storybook's sidebar, expand the **test widget**, check **Coverage**, and run tests from there — this runs the `storybook` project specifically (so it's the same scope as `test:coverage:storybook` above) and gives you a clickable, interactive coverage report right in the browser, file by file, line by line.

This is entirely free — `@storybook/addon-vitest` and the coverage engine (`@vitest/coverage-v8`) are open source, run locally, no account or usage limits. Nothing to configure; both are already installed and wired into `.storybook/main.ts`.

## Lint & type checks

Not part of the two Vitest projects, but run alongside them in CI:

```bash
npm run lint           # eslint .
npx tsc -b --noEmit    # typecheck, no build output
```

## Token & role governance

Design-system-specific checks — not generic tests, but gate the same way in CI:

```bash
npm run tokens:check          # build + diff + validate + contrast, all in one
npm run roles:check:strict    # fails if any component bypasses getRoleColor()
```

See [Roles](?path=/docs/foundations-roles--docs) for what `roles:check` is actually enforcing, and `docs/foundations/TOKENS.md` for the full token build pipeline.

## What CI actually runs

`.github/workflows/ci.yml` runs on **push to any branch** (not just `main` — broadened so feature branches get real signal instead of nothing until merge) and on **pull requests targeting `main`**:

1. `npm ci`
2. `npm run docs:lint`
3. `npm run lint`
4. `npm run tokens:check`
5. `npm test` — both Vitest projects
6. `npm run build`
7. (PR only) `npm run build-storybook`, uploaded as a downloadable artifact

Two more workflows run the same broadened push trigger: `governance.yml` (strict token/role governance) and `commitlint.yml` (conventional-commit message linting). `contrast.yml` runs on both push and PR, but only when `src/**`, `scripts/check-contrast.js`, `package.json`, or `dist/tokens.json` actually changed — see `.github/workflows/*.yml` for the exact trigger conditions on each.

If a PR-only step (Storybook build artifact) is what you need to check locally before pushing, `npm run build-storybook` reproduces it exactly.

---

<Meta title="Foundations/Governance" />

# Governance

This repo enforces three separate, interlocking governance systems. Each one exists to catch a different kind of drift, and each has its own detailed doc — this page is the map between them, with the visual flow each one is missing on its own.

<GovernanceMap />

---

## 1. Token & role governance

**What it protects:** that every color in the codebase traces back to an approved token, through the 3-tier architecture — never a hardcoded hex value.

<TokenGovernanceFlow />

**Needing a new token that doesn't exist yet** is a separate, upstream decision — design/approval, not enforcement. That flow (which layer, who signs off, how long it takes) is fully mapped in **`docs/TOKEN_REQUEST_DECISION_TREE.md`**, with the written process in **`docs/TOKEN_REQUEST_PROCESS.md`**. This diagram is the other half: once a token *does* exist, what stops someone from bypassing it.

### Checked by

| Command | Checks |
|---|---|
| `npm run roles:check:strict` | Any component importing `tokens.*` or `semanticColors.*` directly, a dangling `--role-*` variable, or a hex literal in `src/components/ui/` source |
| `npm run tokens:check` | Token build succeeds, no unauthorized primitive diff, DTCG export valid, WCAG contrast on every enforced pair |
| `npm run governance:ci` | Every gate below, bundled — this is what `governance.yml` runs in CI |

Full architecture, naming rule, and dark-mode mechanics: [Roles](?path=/docs/foundations-roles--docs), [Colors](?path=/docs/foundations-colors--docs), and **`docs/foundations/TOKENS.md`**.

---

## 1b. The gates that check the gates

**What it protects:** that a green result means something.

Every gate in this repo that has ever been wrong was wrong the same way — it
measured something *adjacent* to what it claimed, and reported green while the
real defect shipped. The axe gate once ran **zero** checks across every story.
The role gate parsed **6 of 55** role names. The registry gate checked index
entries rather than dependency edges. A published release shipped an
`index.d.ts` that did not compile, with all eight gates green.

A green gate is indistinguishable from a disabled one unless something asserts
otherwise. So two harnesses do the asserting, and both run in `governance:ci`.

| Command | Checks |
|---|---|
| `npm run gates:selftest` | Writes a probe containing one real violation per gate, runs the gate, and requires it to exit non-zero **and name the probe**. Exiting non-zero alone is not evidence — a crash, a malformed probe, or an unrelated pre-existing violation all look like a healthy gate |
| `npm run metrics:selftest` | The same idea for the 14 `ds:score` metrics, in **both** directions: a change that should move a metric must move it, and one that should *not* must leave it exactly alone |
| `npm run ds:score` | The health score itself — 14 frozen formulas grouped by goal (development readiness, governance, scalable global system, AI-agent readiness), readable at any git revision so history is backfillable |

The second direction is the one that earns its keep. A metric is a *number*,
and a number can move for the wrong reason: `prop_docs` was once satisfied by
14 docblocks sitting in **empty interface bodies**, which react-docgen cannot
turn into a prop description. The metric moved 44 → 80 while the thing it names
did not budge. Only a probe asserting "this change must *not* count" catches
that.

Adding a gate means adding its probe; adding a metric means adding both of its
probes. That is deliberate friction.

---

## 2. CI quality gates

**What it protects:** that nothing broken — a failing test, a type error, an undocumented token change, a bad commit message — reaches `main`, regardless of which branch it was written on.

<CIGatesFlow />

Push triggers are deliberately **not** `main`-only — this repo does substantial work directly on feature branches, so every branch gets real signal instead of nothing until merge.

**Reproduce any of this locally** before pushing — the exact command for each step is on [Testing](?path=/docs/foundations-testing--docs), and the README's CI & Quality Gates section has the full failure cheatsheet.

---

## 3. Documentation governance

**What it protects:** against exactly what already happened once in this repo — ~70 one-off status reports and build summaries accumulating at the repo root because nothing told anyone where a new doc belonged. `docs:check-sprawl` is the mechanical backstop; the decision ladder below is what actually prevents a new doc from needing to be moved later.

<DocPlacementFlow />

The mechanical gate (`docs:check-sprawl`, run as part of `docs:lint` in every CI run) only catches the literal failure mode — a new `.md` file landing at repo root outside the five allowlisted files. It can't enforce "does an existing doc already cover this" or "has this doc gone stale" — those need judgment, which is what the ladder above is for. Full text version, with the actual list of examples this rule already fixed: **`CLAUDE.md` → Documentation Governance**.

---

## Where each system's detail lives

| System | This page has | Full detail |
|---|---|---|
| Token & role | Enforcement flow | `docs/foundations/TOKENS.md`, `docs/TOKEN_REQUEST_PROCESS.md`, `docs/TOKEN_REQUEST_DECISION_TREE.md` |
| CI gates | Trigger + pipeline flow | [Testing](?path=/docs/foundations-testing--docs), README → CI & Quality Gates |
| Documentation | Decision-ladder flow | `CLAUDE.md` → Documentation Governance, `docs/README.md` |

_This page mirrors `docs/GOVERNANCE.md` (same content, rendered as Mermaid diagrams there for GitHub — this version renders as MDS components so it stays on-brand and theme-aware in Storybook). Keep both in sync if the flows change._

<Meta title="Foundations/Changelog" />

# Changelog

Every released version of the design system, and what changed in it.

This page renders [`CHANGELOG.md`](https://github.com/mmctech/MarshDesignSystem/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md)
directly from the repository — it is not a hand-kept copy, so the two can
never disagree. Nothing below is written by hand.

## How entries get here

Entries are generated from **conventional commit messages**, so the commit
you write *is* the changelog entry. There is no separate step to remember,
and no way for a change to ship undocumented as long as it follows the
format.

```
<type>(<scope>): <subject>

feat(components): add a size prop to Badge
fix(theme): repair the border-radius scale
```

`commitlint` enforces this at commit time (see **Foundations → Governance**),
which is why an invalid type, an unknown scope, or a capitalised subject is
rejected before a commit lands.

The `type` decides which section an entry appears under:

| Commit type | Section |
| --- | --- |
| `feat` | Features |
| `fix` | Bug Fixes |
| `perf` | Performance |
| `refactor` | Refactoring |
| `docs` | Documentation |
| `build` | Build System |
| `ci` | Continuous Integration |
| `test` | Tests |
| `chore` | Chores |

Cutting a release runs `npm run release` (standard-version), which reads the
commits since the last tag, works out the next semver number from their
types, writes them into `CHANGELOG.md`, and tags the result.

**Work that has been merged but not yet released does not appear below** —
it lands here on the next release. To see what is currently unreleased,
compare `main` against the latest tag.
